copy.title: Series pitch: comps
copy.body: Bottom of the Ninth is a half-hour mockumentary about the front office of the worst minor-league team in America, which has one season to sell 3,000 tickets or the team moves to a casino parking lot. It sits between Jury Duty Presents and Shrinking: talking-head, character-driven comedy with a bright, healing center. Its touchstones are Ted Lasso, Abbott Elementary, Parks and Recreation and Bull Durham, so the tone is workplace warmth with baseball underneath. Further comps include Reservation Dogs for deadpan and community, Mythic Quest for workplace comedy that knows its genre, and Welcome to Wrexham for sport as a community story. The Bear shows how far a workplace comedy grounded in operational realism can reach (Top 0.79%), though its fit is lower at 0.63. The audience skews 35–44 (+0.18) and 55+ (+0.10), with an even gender split. [word count]

copy.title: Who it's for
copy.body: The audience is adult and educated, and its taste descriptors include baseball, financial literacy, corporate greed, kindness and vulnerability. That suits a show about a team that a casino lot could replace. Age skews 35–44 (+0.18) and 55+ (+0.10), and 30–34 under-indexes (-0.56). Gender is even (female -0.02, male 0.02). The same audience also likes Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story, Champions, John Prine, Paul Simon and New York Yankees. Emerging markets include Louisville, Washington DC, Burlington, Atlanta, Portland and Albuquerque. This is aggregate taste, not a forecast.

kit.headline: Ted Lasso and Abbott Elementary warmth with Parks and Recreation workplace mockumentary structure and Bull Durham baseball, sized to sit near Jury Duty Presents and Shrinking.
kit.summary: Bottom of the Ninth is a feel-good mockumentary workplace comedy set in baseball, anchored by Ted Lasso, Abbott Elementary, Parks and Recreation and Bull Durham. The closest comps are Jury Duty Presents and Shrinking, which pair talking-head, character-driven comedy with a bright, healing tone. Lead with the Jury Duty Presents meets Shrinking line, then use The Bear as evidence of how large a workplace comedy with operational realism can get. The audience over-indexes at 35–44 and 55+, and its taste runs to baseball, financial literacy and kindness.
